response.description_long:
Shipglass is a feature management platform built around a simple premise: the deploy should not be the moment of risk. Wrap any change in a flag, roll it out to 1 percent of users, watch the metrics, and ramp or roll it back without another deploy. The company frames the alternative in terms every engineer recognizes — the change is merged, the deploy is out, and the only way back is another deploy, reviewed, rebuilt, and rolled out, while the bug burns. Flags, in Shipglass's telling, turn release into a runtime decision by separating deploy from release: teams merge continuously and release deliberately, by cohort, region, or plan, with an instant kill switch instead of a hotfix train.

Mechanically, the product leans on local evaluation. SDKs for 12 languages evaluate flags locally from a streamed ruleset, so evaluation adds well under 1 millisecond and works offline. Targeting rules combine user attributes, cohorts, and percentage rollouts — 1 percent of free-plan users in Germany, everyone in the beta cohort, 50 percent of new signups. Percentage bucketing is deterministic per user, so a user who saw a feature yesterday sees it today at the same rollout stage, consistently across sessions and services. Cohorts can sync from a data warehouse or be built from attributes, and entitlement flags can mirror billing plans so plan gating lives in one place. An edge network with points of presence on every populated continent keeps rulesets within 50 milliseconds of users worldwide, and a flag change published in the dashboard reaches every connected SDK in under a second globally.

The SDK lineup is first-party across JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, Kotlin, Swift, Ruby, PHP, C#, Rust, and Elixir. Server SDKs stream over SSE; mobile SDKs fetch on foreground and cache, tuned for battery life and app-store constraints. If the stream drops, an SDK serves the last ruleset it saw and reconciles on reconnect, while a brand-new process falls back to bundled defaults the customer defines. The site is explicit that the edge serves rulesets only and evaluation stays in your process, so the request path never waits on Shipglass.

Beyond rollout, Shipglass folds in audit, hygiene, and experimentation without asking teams to stand up a separate stack. Every flag change — who, what, when, from which environment — lands in an immutable audit log streamable to a SIEM, and approvals can be required per environment so production ramps need a second pair of eyes while staging stays fast. The platform surfaces stale flags automatically: fully ramped for 30 days, evaluated but never varying, or referenced in code but never evaluated, each with a cleanup pull request generated for supported languages. Any rollout can become an A/B test by attaching a metric; Shipglass computes lift with confidence intervals, and the results view shows lift, confidence intervals, and sample-size progress. Guardrail metrics watch error rates and latency during every ramp whether or not it is called an experiment — a ramp that degrades a guardrail pauses itself and pages the flag owner.

The stated audience is product engineering teams that ship daily, with common first uses in risky migrations, tiered entitlements, and gradual mobile rollouts where app-store review makes rollback expensive. The site names three concrete patterns. In the migration pattern, the new database path is wrapped in a flag, reads ramp to 1 percent, results are compared in the shadow, the ramp goes to 100, and the old path is deleted — with an instant kill switch the whole way. In the entitlement pattern, plan tiers become flags so packaging changes ship without a deploy. In the mobile pattern, the feature ships dark in the binary, app review happens once, and the release ramps server-side over days, so a crash spike is answered with a toggle rather than a resubmission.

Pricing is published and straightforward: Free covers up to 5 seats, unlimited flags, all SDKs, and one production environment. Pro is $12 per seat per month and adds unlimited environments, approvals, experiments, stale-flag cleanup, and the audit log. Enterprise adds SAML, custom roles, and a dedicated single-tenant environment, billed annually. Seats count humans who log in; service accounts and CI are free. The free tier's unlimited flags is described as a deliberate stance against per-flag pricing, which the founders regard as a tax on exactly the discipline flags require.

Shipglass was founded in Denver in 2021, and the team of 27 previously built release tooling at large consumer-software companies. Founders Casey Morrow and Ben Alvarez ran release engineering where a bad Friday deploy meant a weekend, and built the first version as a tool they had hacked together twice before at previous employers — this time with the evaluation engine, the audit trail, and the cleanup story done properly. The company's own positioning names its favorite competitor as the homegrown alternative: a config table and a prayer. Its engineering blog, particularly a config-table autopsy and a writeup on deterministic bucketing across services, circulates among platform teams, and the company publishes its edge network's ruleset delivery latency on its status page.
